text: Musical ontology strikes me as a field built on a category error. We try to locate the work as if it's a fixed object, but music is fundamentally an event. You can't pin down an event the way you pin down a sculpture.

The score is not the music; it's a set of instructions for generating the music. But if you take that seriously, the identity of the musical work becomes incredibly fragile. Every performance is technically a variation.

If two performances of the same Beethoven sonata are structurally identical in notes but phrased differently, do they constitute the same work? The repeatability problem means our definition of musical identity is full of holes.

It's strange that we accept recording as the definitive version of a track. Once tape allowed for a single, repeatable instance, the philosophy of music shifted from studying the composition to studying the frozen artifact.

Enactivism suggests that music doesn't exist out there in the air, nor just inside the head, but in the physical engagement between player, instrument, and listener. The meaning isn't transmitted; it's enacted together in real time.
If the pitch percept is a construct, as we saw with missing fundamentals, then the musical work itself must be seen as a joint construction. It requires an active listener to complete the circuit.

I've been thinking about the limits of cross-cultural universals. Some studies find global similarities in lullabies and dance music, suggesting an evolutionary basis. But the way those structures are parsed is subject to radical perceptual divergence.

What we call musical meaning in Western art music is intensely tied to harmonic resolution. But in traditions where drone or rhythmic cycle dominates, the meaning is located entirely differently. Our ontology is parochial.

To say a performance was faithful to the score implies the score is the ultimate arbiter of truth. But notation is notoriously low-resolution. It leaves out almost everything that makes music sound musical.
If the work is neither the score nor the performance, maybe it exists only as an ideal object. A Platonic form that every performance merely approximates. But that feels like a philosophical retreat.
Temporal experience is what makes music so difficult to theorize. You can't observe the whole piece at once. Memory and anticipation are the only ways the structure holds together in the mind.

Enactivism dissolves the work-concept completely. If music is an activity jointly constituted by participants, then there is no object left to preserve. This makes traditional musicology very uncomfortable.

Is it possible to have a philosophy of music that doesn't implicitly privilege the composer over the performer? Our institutional language still treats interpreters as secondary agents, mere channels for the real work.

The perceptual divergence finding is critical. A chord that sounds resolved to one listener might sound incomplete to another raised in a different tuning culture. Meaning is inextricably bound to exposure.
I keep returning to this idea: musical meaning cannot simply be linguistic. It doesn't denote anything in the real world. So how does it manage to communicate such specific affective states?

The concept of repeatability requires agreement on what parameters matter. If pitch and rhythm are identical, we say it's the same piece, even if the timbre is totally changed. Try telling that to a spectral composer.

I'm struggling with the claim that there are cross-cultural universals in music. Even if you find common acoustic features, assuming they carry the same meaning assumes a universal listening subject, which might be a myth.
When we recall music, we often don't recall it linearly in real-time. We can jump around a symphony in our head. Does that mean the temporal experience is somehow flattened in memory?

The work identity of a free improvisation is paradoxical. It only exists once. If you somehow transcribed and replayed it perfectly, you would destroy its fundamental nature, which was its spontaneity.
Musicology is only just starting to grapple with enactivism. It forces you to stop looking at dots on a page and start looking at bodies moving the air in a room.
If pitch fusion works differently based on cultural training, then the very boundary of what counts as a single note is subjective. The divergence happens at the lowest level of perception.
The score versus performance debate assumes they are in opposition. But a score is just a highly specialized communication technology designed to compress musical intention across centuries.
The problem with searching for musical universals is that you often end up proving that all humans have the same ears. Acoustic facts are universal; the meaning extracted from them is not.
Music as an experience of time is completely unique. A book can be put down, a painting glanced at, but a piece of music demands you inhabit its temporal flow at its own dictated speed.
There's a persistent tension in the philosophy of music: is music an object to be analyzed or an action to be participated in? The language we use heavily slants toward the former.
If the meaning is socially constructed, why does a dominant-seventh chord physically demand resolution? There seems to be an acoustic floor to these ontological questions.
Enactivism suggests the listener isn't passive. Listening is a kind of silent performance. The motor cortex lights up when trained musicians hear a piece, even if they aren't moving.
Maybe musical work identity is better understood functionally. A performance is an instance of the work if it serves the same function in the community that the composition intended.

The idea of the musical work as an autonomous, repeatable object only emerged around the 18th century, tied to music publishing. Before that, music was an event. We naturalize a very recent historical paradigm.
To truly study temporal experience in music, you have to measure how long a listener's present moment extends. Does it cover just the current phrase, or does it hold the memory of the exposition?
We use the term meaning too loosely. When music means something, it's not pointing to a referent. It's creating an internal state that has a shape, a contour. It's a syntactic meaning, not semantic.

The fact that different cultures parse meter differently—a 7/8 cycle feeling uncomfortably lopsided to a Western ear but completely stable elsewhere—is a stark example of perceptual divergence shaping cognition.
The score is a lossy compression format. You decompress it through a human performer, and the decompression algorithm is their entire lifetime of practice and cultural exposure.

Philosophy of music has spent way too long worrying about whether John Cage's 4'33" is music. Ontologically, it's more interesting to ask why a Beethoven symphony played by MIDI feels like it's missing the point.
How much can a piece change before it's a new piece? Jazz standards stretch work identity to its absolute limit, maintaining only a ghost of the original harmonic skeleton.

Cross-cultural research frequently uses MIDI to eliminate performative variation, but that accidentally eliminates the exact timbral micro-cues that carry the music's meaning in many traditions. It's a methodological blind spot.
Music is a structured intervention in how we sense time passing. That temporal experience is why music is so intimately linked to movement and dance—it synchronizes internal clocks.
I'm fascinated by the idea of an ideal object in musical ontology. Nobody has ever heard the ideal St. Matthew Passion, yet every conductor acts as though they are trying to reach it.

The repeatability problem disappears entirely if you abandon the concept of the work. If every performance is an original act merely referencing a prior act, music becomes much closer to oral storytelling.
Enactivism posits that perception is not something that happens to us, but something we do. Hearing a melody is actively tracing its shape with the mind, participating in its unfolding.

If musical meaning was just about acoustic physics, there wouldn't be perceptual divergence. But a Javanese gamelan sounds out-of-tune to someone expecting equal temperament, and perfectly tuned to an expert.
Is a recording of a performance an instance of the musical work, or a representation of it? The distinction matters when we confuse the fixed audio file with the living composition.
Think about how the pitch percept from those missing fundamentals taught us that the brain fills in the gaps. Our sense of musical form works the same way—we project continuity across silence.

Exploring the philosophy of music sometimes feels like trying to hold water. The parameters of pitch, time, and timbre are clear, but how they spontaneously generate profound emotion remains fundamentally mysterious.
Maybe the concept of the work is just a legal and economic fiction designed to assign copyright, and has nothing to do with how music actually functions in the brain or the room.

When you experience a piece of music temporally, you're constantly evaluating the past against the present. A minor chord heard at the beginning means something entirely different when heard after a long development.
What if cross-cultural universals in music are just the lowest common denominator? The really deep meaning might only be accessible when you learn the specific culturally-bound syntax.
A score is an incomplete schematic. The performer must provide the unwritten nuances of timing and dynamics. The work literally does not exist until it is interpreted.
I wonder if the drive for perfect repeatability in classical music is an anxiety about loss. If we can lock the notes down perfectly, maybe the piece won't change. But pieces always change.
Ultimately, musical ontology is wrestling with the fact that music is both intensely physical—vibrating air—and utterly immaterial. It disappears the moment it's created, but its structure stays.
